idiom_name: discriminated union of operation objects + exhaustive switch with a never check
implementation_notes: A union of object types sharing a literal `kind`/`type` field is the algebra, `switch (op.kind)` narrows it branch by branch, and a default branch assigning `op` to `never` turns a forgotten operation into a compile error - the closest TypeScript gets to exhaustiveness, and it only holds while the union stays closed, `strictNullChecks` is on, and no arm escapes through `any`. Programs are plain JSON-friendly values: equality-assertable in tests, loggable, serializable across workers. Types are erased, so the interpreter is a runtime function and any program arriving as data must be validated (zod/io-ts) before interpretation - the type-level contract protects only in-process construction. Where operations carry no data and only the tag matters, a string-literal union is the lighter local idiom.
pitfalls: The `never` assignment only fails the build while the union stays closed: widening it with an index signature, a base type with `string` kind, or an `as any` disables the check.
Programs arriving from outside the process are typeless data - validate them (zod/io-ts) before the interpreter runs, or a hostile payload chooses an unexpected kind.
Optional properties in union members weaken narrowing; keep the discriminant required on every member.
